883.title: Chardi kala in the century
883.hook: a people hunted for decades sang at night
883.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Kirtan Sohila before sleep, and the Ardas closes with a wish for chardi kala through the Name and the good of all; Sikhs greet hardship with the phrase chardi kala as an ideal of spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, visiting the sites: gurdwaras in the fields at Kahnuwan and Kup Rahira. Your line was the places remember. What hard place near you did you find out about? Day eight hundred eighty-three.

Two words sit near the very end of the Ardas, just before the wish for the good of all: chardi kala. Sikhs say them to one another as well, in easy times and hard ones. On an easy day they can sound like a slogan. But Sikhs remember decades when they were hunted and outnumbered, and in the stories of those camps, rising spirits had to mean something by nightfall. Today: chardi kala in the century.
screen: `TWO WORDS NEAR THE END OF THE ARDAS.` → `SAID IN EASY TIMES AND HARD.` → `TESTED BY NIGHTFALL IN THE CAMPS.`

segments.voice: Chardi kala. Sikhs translate it as rising spirits, or ever-ascending spirit. It's not the same as cheerfulness. It's a spirit that stays turned upward when everything outside is turned down. Three things show what it meant in the hard century. First, the night prayer itself. Sikhs end the day with Kirtan Sohila, and its first hymn, by Guru Nanak, speaks of the house where the Creator's praises are sung and reflected on, and asks that the song of praise be sung there. Here in paraphrase. The riders had no house. Tradition says they sang it anyway, quietly, in camps without lamps, and the camp became the house. Second, back to the Ardas. The half-line before the good of all joins two things: Nanak's Name, and chardi kala. In the prayer, rising spirits aren't a personality trait. They come from the Name. A rider didn't have to feel brave to have chardi kala; he had to keep remembering. Third, the humor, the same camp speech the Nihangs still keep. Tradition says the camps kept a joking way of talking about their own hardship, giving poor things grand names, laughing at hunger rather than letting it win. Joking about yourself while the world tries to erase you is its own kind of courage. Put the three together: a song at night, a Name to lean on, a joke at your own expense. None of it changed the danger. It changed how the people in it carried it. Hunted for decades, they still sang.

segments.voice: Two minutes with one line. Choose a line you know that lifts you: a hymn, a song from childhood, a verse, even a lullaby. If you pray, it could be Waheguru, said slowly. Breathe, and say or hum the line under your breath, once, then again. Don't perform it. Let it be quiet, the way it would be in a camp with no lamps. Notice whether anything in you rises, even a little. If nothing does, that's fine. They sang either way. The bell holds the time.
Chardi kala in the century. Rising spirits that came from the Name, kept in the camps with a night prayer and a joke at their own expense. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: they still sang. Tonight, before sleep, sing or say one line you love, even in a whisper, even on a bad day. Day eight hundred eighty-three.

884.title: Women who kept the homes
884.hook: while men rode, women farmed, hid, fed and taught
884.howItsDone: Sikh women take the name Kaur at initiation and share the same standing in the sangat; at home, families teach children the daily prayers and Gurmukhi, and Sikh talks honor the women who kept households through the persecutions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chardi kala in the century: a night prayer in a camp with no lamps. Your line was they still sang. What line did you sing or say before sleep? Day eight hundred eighty-four.

A knock at a farmhouse door after dark. Two riders, exhausted, horses blown. The man of the house is away with a band of his own. The woman who opens the door has children asleep inside and soldiers searching the district. She has seconds to decide. The stories of this century follow the riders: the raids, the sieges, the names of chiefs. But every rider came from a home, and somebody kept that home standing while he was gone. Today: women who kept the homes.
screen: `A KNOCK AFTER DARK.` → `SECONDS TO DECIDE.` → `EVERY RIDER CAME FROM A HOME.`

segments.voice: Start with what tradition remembers they did, because it's a long list. They farmed. With the men riding, the fields still had to be plowed, watered, harvested, and the grain hidden from tax collectors and raiders. They hid people. Tradition tells of riders sheltered in village houses, in grain stores, behind a wall of fodder, with a woman at the door answering questions calmly. They fed. The grain that reached the camps came from somebody's kitchen. And they taught. Tradition says that with gurdwaras watched or seized, the prayers and the Gurmukhi letters passed from mothers to children at home, by heart. That's one way a scripture survives persecution: at kitchen tables. Now set that beside the Guru Granth Sahib. Guru Nanak, in a passage Sikhs return to, asks why anyone would speak ill of woman, from whom kings are born. Here in paraphrase. He describes life itself as running through women: we're born of them, we're bound to them, the world goes on through them. And Sikh tradition says the Khalsa gave women their own name, Kaur, alongside the men's Singh, the same initiation, the same standing before the Guru. Not long ago on this path you met the mothers in the governor's prison who kept faith. The women who kept the homes had a quieter courage, spread over years of answering the door. The chronicles followed the riders. But the riders had somewhere to come back to, because she held it together.

A mother, a grandmother, an aunt, a teacher, a neighbor, a friend. Picture her doing the ordinary work: the meal, the bills, the phone call to the school, the door opened at the wrong hour. Stay with her face. Notice how much rested on her. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Women who kept the homes. While the riders were away, women farmed, hid them, fed the camps and taught the children the prayers. Today's word.

885.title: What the century teaches
885.hook: faith, courage and shared food carried a small people through
885.howItsDone: Sikhs teach Guru Nanak's way as naam japo, kirat karo and vand chhako, remembering the Name, honest work and sharing, and they tell the stories of the hard century as that way lived under pressure.

segments.voice: Yesterday, women who kept the homes: farming, hiding, feeding, teaching. Your line was she held it together. Who did you thank, and what did you name? Day eight hundred eighty-five.

A saddlebag. Leather, worn soft, small enough to sling behind a rider. If you could open one from the hard century, what would be inside? Some flour, maybe. A little salt. A wrapped bundle with prayers written in Gurmukhi. In the stories, beside a horse and a weapon, that's close to everything a hunted rider owned. And yet the people who carried bags like that came through the century, still a people, still praying, still feeding strangers. So what got them through? Today: what the century teaches.
screen: `A WORN SADDLEBAG.` → `FLOUR, SALT, A BUNDLE OF PRAYERS.` → `WHAT GOT THEM THROUGH?`

segments.voice: Sikhs sum up Guru Nanak's teaching in three short phrases: naam japo, remember the Name; kirat karo, earn honestly; vand chhako, share what you have. Hold them up against the hard century and you'll find them there, with courage standing beside them. The first is faith, the Name. The riders said the morning prayers from memory, opened the Granth wherever they stopped, and sang Kirtan Sohila in camps without lamps. The Ardas ties rising spirits to the Name, and the camps lived that. When everything else could be taken, the Name couldn't. The second is courage. Not the courage of revenge. The Ardas remembers the martyrs by what they endured and names no enemy. The courage the century hands on is the kind that stands, shields the families, rebuilds at the ruins, and answers the door after dark. The third is honest bread, shared. Guru Nanak, in the Guru Granth Sahib, says in paraphrase that the one who earns by work and gives some of it with their own hands has recognized the way. That's kirat and vand in one line. The Khalsa put the cooking pot before the sword, kept a common pot in the forests, and fed whoever came to the fire. Put those three in the saddlebag: a Name, a backbone, a pot. None of them is heavy. All of them can be shared. And none of them needed a building, a treasury or a government to keep going. That's what the century teaches, and it doesn't need a war to apply. On an ordinary Tuesday, the question is the same one the riders lived: what carries you?
screen: `NAAM, KIRAT, VAND.` · `FAITH: THE NAME COULD NOT BE TAKEN.` · `COURAGE THAT STANDS, NOT REVENGE.` · `SHARED FOOD: THE POT BEFORE THE SWORD.` · then, large: `WHAT CARRIES YOU?`

segments.voice: Two minutes to pack your own saddlebag. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself: when things got hard, what actually got me through? Not what should have. What did. A practice, a person, a phrase, a habit of feeding people, a stubbornness you're quietly proud of. Let a few things come up. Then choose three, and name each one silently, the way you'd lay them out on a blanket before a long ride. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
What the century teaches. Faith in the Name, courage without revenge, and food shared even when there's little: three light things that carried a small people through. Today's word.

886.title: The hard century close
886.hook: from Banda to Lahore: the hard century remembered in every Ardas
886.howItsDone: Sikhs say the Ardas standing at the close of prayers and gatherings, and its martyrs' passage remembers by their deeds the Sikhs of the persecutions; the congregation answers Waheguru after it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what the century teaches: the Name, courage without revenge, and a shared pot. Your line was what carries you. Where did you put your three things? Today, we close the hard century. Day eight hundred eighty-six.

Weeks ago on this path, a Guru at Nanded met an ascetic who became Banda, the servant, and rode north with five arrows. Since then: towns taken and lost, a siege in a mud fort, a march to Delhi, a scholar executed for a festival, a humble nawab, forests and deserts, two holocausts, a temple blown up and rebuilt, Sirhind, and chiefs riding into Lahore. A long road. And all of it, Sikhs say, is folded into a few lines they say standing. Today: the hard century close.
screen: `FROM BANDA AND FIVE ARROWS.` → `SIEGES, FORESTS, TWO HOLOCAUSTS.` → `TO CHIEFS RIDING INTO LAHORE.`

segments.voice: Go back to the passage in the Ardas you met a few days back. It remembers Sikhs cut limb from limb, scalped, broken on the wheel, who gave their heads but kept their faith, who kept their hair to the last breath, who gave their lives for the gurdwaras. The prayer doesn't name them. But Sikhs listening hear particular people in those lines. Tradition links cut limb from limb to Bhai Mani Singh, whom you met at the Diwali gathering. Broken on the wheel calls up the father and son, Subeg Singh and Shahbaz Singh. Scalped calls up Bhai Taru Singh, who, tradition says, gave up his scalp rather than his hair. So that's the first thing: much of the century you just walked through is inside the prayer. The second thing is who says it. Not historians. A grandmother at dawn. A child at a school assembly. A family before a long drive. A congregation after a wedding. The hard century isn't kept in archives first. It's kept in the mouths of ordinary people, standing, hands folded. The third thing is the tone. The passage remembers what was endured, and then the Ardas moves on to ask for the Name, for humility, for the good of all. Memory, then asking, then a wish for everyone. That's the shape these weeks have followed too: the servant and his arrows, the hunted years, the ruins, the turn, and a people still singing at the end. All those weeks of story, and the place it lives is a prayer said standing. Remembered in every Ardas.
screen: `THE CENTURY FOLDED INTO THE PRAYER.` · `MANI SINGH, SUBEG, SHAHBAZ, TARU.` · `KEPT BY ORDINARY PEOPLE, STANDING.` · `MEMORY, ASKING, THE GOOD OF ALL.` · then, large: `REMEMBERED IN EVERY ARDAS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the martyrs' part of the Ardas. If you pray the Ardas, you can stand, fold your hands, and say that passage slowly, letting each line call up a face from these weeks. If you don't, sit and let the lines come back as you heard them today: cut limb from limb, broken on the wheel, scalped. After each one, pause for a breath and picture someone who stood. Then, at the end, one breath for the good of all. The bell holds the time.
The hard century close. From Banda's five arrows to chiefs in Lahore, the whole century is folded into the martyrs' passage Sikhs say standing. Today's word.
Your line: remembered in every ardas. Today, tell one story from this century to someone who's never heard it. Tomorrow, the misls begin. Day eight hundred eighty-six.

887.title: What a misl was
887.hook: a misl was a band of equals with its own chief, joined to the others in the Dal Khalsa
887.howItsDone: Sikhs learn about the misls in Sikh histories and at gurdwara talks, and the gurmata, a decision made together in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib, is still part of how the Panth gathers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hard century closed, and its martyrs are remembered in every Ardas. Did a name from those years stay with you? Today a new stretch of the story begins. Day eight hundred eighty-seven.

A rider comes into Amritsar with a few dozen horsemen behind him. Another arrives from the north with his own men, and another from across the river. None of them is king of the others. Each band has its own chief, its own villages, its own way of doing things. But when they reach the Guru's city, they sit down together as one Khalsa. For the next part of this path, those bands are the story. Each one had a name, and the name for the band itself is today's word: misl.
screen: `RIDERS FROM EVERY DIRECTION.` → `EACH BAND WITH ITS OWN CHIEF.` → `ONE KHALSA AT AMRITSAR.`

segments.voice: Here's what a misl was, turned four ways. First, a misl was a band. Tradition says it gathered around a chief, a sardar, who had earned the trust of the riders with him. The band held land and protected the villages under it, and those villages paid it for that protection. Second, a band of equals. In the way Sikh histories tell it, a rider in a misl wasn't the chief's servant. He was a Singh of the Khalsa who had chosen to ride with this sardar, and tradition says he could leave and ride with another. What was won was shared out. The chief led, but he led people who stood on the same ground he did. Third, the misls didn't stand alone. Together they made up the Dal Khalsa, the army of the Khalsa. When a danger was too big for one band, they rode as one. And tradition says that at the great gatherings in Amritsar, the Sarbat Khalsa, the chiefs met before the Guru Granth Sahib and agreed on a gurmata, a resolution in the Guru's presence, which every band was bound by. Fourth, the misls were what the hard century produced. Small bands that had once hidden in forests and deserts now held the countryside. Over the coming days, the path visits the misls one by one: who led them, where they rode, what each became. Some grew strong. Some stayed small. One would one day give rise to a kingdom. But they started in the same place: a band of equals.

Misl. A Sikh band with its own chief, its riders free to join it, joined to the other bands in the Dal Khalsa. Today's word.

888.title: The Bhangi misl
888.hook: the strongest early misl, holding Lahore and Amritsar for a time
888.howItsDone: Sikhs meet the Bhangi misl in Sikh histories and in stories about Lahore and Amritsar, where the band's fort and the great gun are remembered.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the misl: a band with its own chief, joined to the others in the Dal Khalsa. Your line was a band of equals. Whose idea did you let lead? Today, the first band by name. Day eight hundred eighty-eight.

A huge bronze cannon sits on a street in Lahore. Tradition says people in the Punjab once had a nickname for it, a name that had nothing to do with whoever cast it. They named it after the Sikh band that held it: the Bhangis' gun. A band that could keep hold of a gun like that, in a city like Lahore, was no small band. Today: the Bhangi misl.
screen: `A GREAT GUN IN LAHORE.` → `CALLED THE BHANGIS' GUN.` → `A BAND THAT HELD A CITY.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Tradition says it came from one of the band's early leaders, who was fond of bhang, a drink made from hemp, and the nickname stuck to the whole misl. Sikh histories tell it lightly, and the name outlived the habit. That's the first thing: a band can be known by a nickname long after anyone remembers why. The second thing is reach. In the way Sikh histories tell it, the Bhangis grew fast in the years after the hard century. Their chiefs held land across a wide stretch of the Punjab. In Amritsar, tradition says, they built a fort and held parts of the Guru's city. And when the Dal Khalsa took Lahore, Bhangi chiefs were among those who shared the city and ruled it. Lahore and Amritsar: the governor's city and the Guru's city, with one misl's riders in both. The third thing is the gun. Tradition says the Bhangis captured the great cannon, and it stayed with them long enough to carry their name. It became a sign of their strength. And here's the fourth thing, the one in today's line. It didn't last. The Bhangi chiefs who came later were not the riders their fathers had been, as Sikh histories tell it, and they quarreled with each other. In time Lahore passed to another misl's leader, a young man you'll meet later on this path. Amritsar too. Strength gathered in one generation was spent in the next. The Bhangis were real, and they were strong. For a time.
screen: `A NAME THAT CAME FROM A NICKNAME.` · `LAHORE AND AMRITSAR IN BHANGI HANDS.` · `THE GREAT GUN THAT CARRIED THEIR NAME.` · `THE STRENGTH THAT DIDN'T LAST.` · then, large: `STRONG, FOR A TIME.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with strength. Sit, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one thing you're strong in right now: a skill, your health, a friendship, a job you're good at. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
The Bhangi misl. The band named for a nickname, whose chiefs held parts of Lahore and Amritsar and the great gun, until the strength passed. Today's word.
Your line: strong, for a time. Today, when you use a strength you have, use it on something that will outlast you a little: teach it, share it, hand it on. Day eight hundred eighty-eight.

889.title: The Ahluwalia misl
889.hook: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia's misl, later the state of Kapurthala
889.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Jassa Singh Ahluwalia in Sikh histories and gurdwara talks as a leader of the Dal Khalsa, and the Ahluwalia name lives on in families and in the town of Kapurthala.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bhangi misl, with its great gun and its two cities. Your line was strong, for a time. What strength did you hand on? Today, a band that was known for one man. Day eight hundred eighty-nine.

Two hats. That's the problem today's chief had. You've met Jassa Singh Ahluwalia on this path already: the boy who sang kirtan, the young rider Nawab Kapur Singh trained, the man the Khalsa called Sultan-ul-Qaum. Today, look at him from a different side. He had his own band, with its own riders and villages to look after. And he was also the one the chiefs looked to when all the bands rode together. Lead your own people, and lead everyone. Today: the Ahluwalia misl.
screen: `TWO HATS.` → `HIS OWN BAND.` → `AND THE WHOLE DAL KHALSA.`

segments.voice: Four pieces. The first is the name. Tradition says Jassa Singh's family came from a village called Ahlu, near Lahore, and his band took its name from it: Ahluwalia, the ones from Ahlu. The second piece is the first hat. As chief of his own misl, he had riders who had chosen to ride with him and villages that looked to his band for protection. That's the ordinary work of a sardar: keep your people fed, safe and together. The third piece is the second hat. Tradition says that when the bands gathered at Amritsar and rode as the Dal Khalsa, the chiefs put Jassa Singh at the head. Think about what that asks of a man. When the spoils are shared, does his own band get the best? When there's a hard job, does it go to someone else's riders? In the way Sikh histories tell it, the chiefs of other bands trusted him, and that trust is the whole point. A leader of everyone can't lead only for his own. The fourth piece is what the band became. Long after the riding years, the lands of the Ahluwalia misl became the state of Kapurthala, ruled by chiefs who carried the Ahluwalia name. The band outlasted the age of bands. Other misls on this path are remembered for a fort, a flag, a river or a fight. This one is remembered because of who led it, and because the man who led it was trusted beyond it. It's the leader's misl.
screen: `AHLUWALIA: THE ONES FROM AHLU.` · `CHIEF OF HIS OWN BAND.` · `AT THE HEAD OF THE DAL KHALSA.` · `HIS LANDS BECAME KAPURTHALA.` · then, large: `THE LEADER'S MISL.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with a leader. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who has led you well: a coach, a manager, a teacher, an older cousin. Not someone famous, someone whose leading you felt up close. Notice whether they were fair to people who weren't their own. Notice what they did that made you trust them. On each breath, let yourself be thankful for one thing they did. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.

The Ahluwalia misl. Jassa Singh's band from Ahlu, whose lands became Kapurthala. This week: chardi kala in the century, the women who kept the homes, what the century teaches, the hard century's close, the misl, the Bhangis, and the Ahluwalias. Today's word.
Your line: the leader's misl. Today, tell one person who led you well what they did right. Leaders rarely hear it. Day eight hundred eighty-nine.
